 Medicare's standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 in 2027, reducing the amount retirees keep from their Social Security checks. Premiums will rise by 3.2 percent from $202.90 to $209.40 a month, while the annual Part B deductible will increase by $9 to $292, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) announced Tuesday. The change comes as Social Security recipients await a 3.6 percent cost-of-living, or COLA, adjustment in the new year. The premium increase will absorb about 8.7 percent of the average $75 monthly retirement benefit boost, leaving about $68.60 a month before any other deductions. The CMS increases, or more rarely decreases, the amount payable for Part B services every year. The department has said the rise this year owes mainly to "projected increases in healthcare spending." How Medicare Cuts Into Social Security Medicare Part B helps pay for doctors' services, outpatient hospital care, certain home health services, medical equipment and other services. The premium, paid monthly, is deducted from Social Security payments, reducing the overall amount deposited into a beneficiary's bank account. The $75 figure is illustrative, based on average Social Security retirement payments, and how much an individual beneficiary will see their benefits boosted by is based solely on their own payments, though the Medicare cost increase is the same for all enrollees. Therefore, a person who gets a larger boost to their benefits due to the COLA will see a smaller drop in their benefits, while someone who only gets a more modest increase will see more of that absorbed by Medicare premiums. Measured against the 3.6 percent COLA increase, the $6.50 premium hike would take about 12 percent of a $54 raise on a $1,500 benefit, leaving about $47.50, or 88 percent, of the increase. For a $3,000 monthly payment, it would take about 6 percent of the $108 raise, leaving about $101.50, or 94 percent, of the increase. "In terms of cold, hard math, most will be marginally better off," David Kassir, managing director at Manna Wealth Management, told Newsweek. "That's because the 3.6 percent COLA is based on a percentage of one's benefit amount while the $6.50 increase in premiums applies equally (almost) to all. So those receiving more substantial Social Security checks will see dollar-for-dollar increases that more than make up for the higher Part B premium." "But for those receiving less than average benefits, the COLA won't be as generous. And the Part B increase will have a greater impact," he continued. "Flat rate hikes hit hardest those receiving the smallest of Social Security checks. It's a nuance that's often lost in the shuffle." The 2027 premium increase is the first time since 2023 that the Part B percentage increase is smaller than the COLA. Back then, the premium actually fell by 3.1 percent, while Social Security recipients received an outsized 8.7 percent boost to benefits, owing to heightened inflation as the U.S. came out of the coronavirus pandemic. Other Medicare Changes Alongside the Part B premium increase, other healthcare costs will rise for enrollees. The Part A hospital deductible, which covers inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facilities, hospice, inpatient rehabilitation and some home health care, will rise by $40, from $1,736 in 2026 to $1,776 in 2027, while the daily coinsurance for longer hospital stays and skilled nursing facility care will also go up. However, 99 percent of Medicare beneficiaries do not pay a Part A premium because they or their spouse have enough Medicare-covered work history, according to the CMS. What Happens Next The COLA and new Medicare premiums will start in January 2027. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
